slides.title: MDMA increases social approach in octopuses
body: **MDMA**, 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, altered social approach in the California two-spot octopus, _Octopus bimaculoides_. Edsinger and Dölen compared exploration before and after drug exposure. A three-chamber aquarium offered access to an unfamiliar male, an unfamiliar object and an empty central compartment. The other octopus remained inside a perforated container. This arrangement permitted social investigation while preventing a fight between the animals.

After MDMA treatment, subjects spent more time in the compartment containing the male. Their time near the unfamiliar object did not increase correspondingly. Transitions between compartments also failed to increase. The behavioral shift therefore concerned the social stimulus rather than a general rise in swimming activity. The same animal supplied a pre-treatment comparison for its later exploration.

The experimental change included direct investigation of the container holding the other octopus. Before treatment, contact was often restricted to an extended arm. After treatment, animals used more extensive contact involving the ventral body surface. **Social approach** here means measurable proximity and contact with another individual. The experiment connects a psychoactive substance to a change in an otherwise predominantly solitary animal’s social behavior.

slides.title: Social contact includes a change in exploratory touch
body: The identity of a social partner affected untreated octopus exploration. Both male and female subjects approached an unfamiliar female more readily than an unfamiliar male. A **conspecific** is another individual of the same species. The study compared conspecific investigation with exploration of a novel object. Partner sex consequently formed part of the biological stimulus rather than an interchangeable feature of the apparatus.

The perforated container allowed visual, tactile and chemical information to pass between animals. The subject could approach or withdraw throughout the 30 min session. Investigators measured time in each compartment separately. Time in the central compartment was similar across the partner-sex conditions. Differences were concentrated in the relative allocation of exploration to social and object compartments.

MDMA testing used the less-preferred male social stimulus. Drug exposure increased the time allocated to that compartment and changed the pattern of bodily contact. Proximity and touch therefore supplied complementary descriptions of the response. The object compartment retained a separate measure of non-social exploration. Social behavior in this preparation depended jointly on the partner being encountered and the subject’s pharmacological state.

slides.title: The octopus serotonin transporter retains a drug target
body: **Serotonin** is a signaling molecule used by neurons in many animal lineages. A **transporter** is a membrane protein that moves a substance across the cell membrane. The serotonin transporter, abbreviated **SERT**, participates in clearing released serotonin from extracellular space. MDMA interacts with this transporter in mammals. The octopus study examined whether the corresponding protein retained relevant molecular features.

The investigators identified two octopus copies of the transporter gene family corresponding to vertebrate SLC6A4. Their analysis compared protein sequences across animal groups. The transporter contains multiple membrane-spanning segments that form a binding pocket. A short region of transmembrane segment 6 implicated in MDMA binding was identical in the compared human and octopus sequences. Other parts of the proteins were more divergent.

The molecular comparison and the behavioral experiment concerned different levels of organization. Sequence conservation identified a plausible shared drug target. Pharmacological treatment then altered social investigation in the living octopus. The study proposes that ancient serotonergic machinery can modulate social behavior despite major differences in brain organization. The precise octopus neurons mediating the response were not localized by these experiments.

slides.title: Caffeine strengthens honeybee odor memory
body: Honeybees, _Apis mellifera_, encounter **caffeine**, a plant alkaloid, in some floral nectars. An **alkaloid** is a nitrogen-containing natural compound that can affect animal physiology. Wright and colleagues paired a floral odor with a sucrose reward. Some rewards also contained caffeine within the range found in nectar. The learned response was extension of the proboscis, the bee’s feeding apparatus.

During testing, the odor was presented without the reward. A bee that extended its proboscis had retained the odor–reward association. Caffeine-treated bees were more likely to respond at later memory tests than bees trained with sucrose alone. The difference persisted at 24 h and 72 h. At the longer retention intervals, caffeine approximately tripled the likelihood of remembering the rewarded scent.

The treatment changed memory even though the odor itself was unchanged. The plant-derived compound accompanied ingestion of the reward during learning. Later odor presentation could then guide behavior after caffeine was no longer being supplied as a reward. **Retention** refers to the persistence of a learned association over time. A nectar constituent can therefore alter the future attractiveness of a flower’s sensory identity.

slides.title: Kenyon-cell responses link caffeine to learned value
body: The honeybee **mushroom bodies** contain Kenyon cells, neurons involved in associative learning. Wright and colleagues recorded electrical responses from these cells in an isolated brain preparation. **Acetylcholine** is an excitatory transmitter in this insect circuit. Applying it produced a depolarizing response, a shift of membrane voltage toward neuronal activation. Caffeine increased the responsiveness of the recorded Kenyon cells.

The study tested caffeine at 100 μM, a concentration relevant to the measured nectar range. Caffeine depolarized the membrane and altered responses to acetylcholine. The investigators also examined an antagonist of adenosine receptors. An **antagonist** blocks the action of a signaling molecule at its receptor. The pharmacological comparison supported adenosine-receptor antagonism as a route through which caffeine changed neuronal excitability.

Enhanced excitability supplies a cellular connection to the stronger odor memory measured in behaving bees. A learned odor activates neural pathways carrying information about the flower. Changing the responsiveness of memory-associated neurons can alter the consequences of that input. The physiological experiment measured voltage responses rather than a bee’s choice of flowers. Together with the conditioning experiment, it links nectar chemistry, neuronal activity and later reward-related behavior.

slides.title: High caffeine concentrations trigger rejection
body: A useful nectar concentration must affect the bee without making the reward unacceptable. Wright and colleagues measured caffeine in nectars of coffee and citrus plants. Those concentrations were below the levels that strongly deterred feeding. They then tested bees with sucrose solutions containing progressively more caffeine. Acceptance declined as the concentration rose above the natural nectar range.

The feeding assay measured proboscis extension after contact with the solution. Increasing sucrose concentration changed the acceptance of caffeine-containing solutions. Sweetness and the deterrent compound therefore contributed jointly to the feeding response. Caffeine above approximately 1 mM was increasingly rejected in the tested mixtures. The same chemical could enhance memory at lower concentrations and discourage consumption at higher concentrations.

These effects act at different stages of a foraging visit. Acceptance determines whether a bee consumes the nectar that it encounters. Memory changes the probability that the bee subsequently responds to the associated scent. A concentration producing rejection cannot supply the same repeated feeding experience as an accepted reward. The measured nectar concentrations occupy a range in which pharmacological effects can occur without strong feeding deterrence.

slides.title: Repeated cocaine changes honeybee responsiveness
body: Repeated cocaine treatment produced **tolerance** in honeybees, meaning a smaller response to a later drug challenge. Søvik and colleagues applied cocaine topically to foraging bees. A larger challenge dose impaired locomotion and the ability to right the body. The **righting reflex** is the coordinated action that restores an overturned animal to its normal orientation. Researchers measured how rapidly bees lost this ability after treatment.

Bees previously given repeated low-dose cocaine were less affected by the later challenge. Their locomotor impairment was reduced relative to drug-naive comparison bees. Vehicle-treated and sham-handled groups separated the drug effect from application and handling. The repeated exposure was administered by the investigators. This experiment measured physiological adaptation rather than voluntary selection of cocaine.

Cocaine interferes with the reuptake of **biogenic amines**, transmitters including dopamine, serotonin and octopamine in insects. Reuptake normally removes released transmitter from extracellular space through membrane transporters. Whole-brain amine measurements did not detect a corresponding treatment-related change in total amine content. Behavioral adaptation can occur while the total amount measured across the brain remains similar. Local transmitter release and receptor responses are distinct from the size of the whole-brain chemical pool.

slides.title: Nicotine alters bumblebee choices between flowers
body: Bumblebees, _Bombus terrestris_, encountered nicotine in an artificial-flower choice task. **Nicotine** is a plant alkaloid that acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Baracchi and colleagues offered flower types with equal sucrose rewards. One type also contained nicotine and the other did not. This arrangement separated the compound’s contribution from a difference in the available sugar reward.

The investigators tested 1 ppm, 2.5 ppm and 50 ppm nicotine. Here **ppm**, parts per million, expresses the concentration of nicotine in the solution. Bees preferred the 1 ppm nicotine-associated flowers over equally rewarded nicotine-free alternatives. At 2.5 ppm, their choices were closer to an equal division. The much higher 50 ppm concentration deterred visits to the nicotine-containing flowers.

Low and high concentrations consequently produced different patterns of choice. Nectar-relevant nicotine concentrations were not automatically rejected as toxins. High concentrations reduced attraction even though sugar remained available. The preference experiment measured repeated visits by freely moving individual bees. A flower’s pharmacological composition can alter foraging choices independently of its caloric reward.

slides.title: Nicotine changes acquisition of floral associations
body: Learning a flower’s color allows a bumblebee to direct later visits toward a rewarding source. Baracchi and colleagues assigned sucrose to one flower color and water to another. Some bees received nicotine with the sucrose reward. The other color remained unrewarding throughout the acquisition phase. **Acquisition** is the development of the association through repeated experience.

Bees in all treatment groups improved their choices across visits. Nicotine at 2.5 ppm accelerated the acquisition of the rewarded color. The 1 ppm and 50 ppm treatments did not produce the same clear acceleration. Equal initial performance separated this later divergence from a starting preference for the rewarded color. By the end of training, performance was high across the groups.

Nicotine altered the rate at which reward information guided choices. The effect depended on concentration rather than increasing steadily with dose. An aversive concentration and a naturally encountered concentration could have different consequences for behavior. The experiment followed individual sequences of visits rather than testing a single approach. Drug exposure during feeding therefore changed the development of a sensory association used during foraging.

slides.title: A learned flower preference persists after reversal
body: **Reversal learning** requires an animal to change a previously successful choice after reward contingencies change. The bumblebee experiment switched which flower color supplied sucrose. The previously rewarded color then supplied water. No nicotine was added to the rewards during this reversal phase. The researchers could therefore measure the consequences of the bees’ earlier nicotine experience.

All groups initially continued to visit the formerly rewarding color. Bees trained with nicotine changed their choices more slowly, particularly after the 50 ppm treatment. Their earlier association persisted despite the loss of its sugar reward. The effect concerned updating the value of a familiar sensory cue. Faster initial acquisition and flexible reversal were consequently separable components of learning.

**Flower constancy** is the tendency to keep visiting a particular flower type. Earlier nicotine exposure increased persistence with that type when it became a poor source of reward. A stable preference can benefit a plant receiving repeated visits. The same persistence becomes costly to a bee when the reward distribution changes. The experiment connects a nectar compound to the balance between retaining an association and updating it through new experience.

slides.title: Ant foraging separates learning from running speed
body: Argentine ants, _Linepithema humile_, repeatedly searched an open arena for a sucrose reward. Galante and colleagues used this task to measure caffeine’s effect on foraging. An ant left the nest, located food and returned before making another journey. Researchers recorded the route and the time required to reach the reward. These measurements distinguished efficient navigation from simply moving faster.

The reward contained 0 ppm, 25 ppm, 250 ppm or 2000 ppm caffeine. The initial foodward journey occurred before the ant had consumed its first experimental reward. Later journeys followed ingestion and experience of the reward’s location. This sequence made repeated visits central to the comparison. Ants could acquire information about the arena while encountering the assigned caffeine concentration.

Moderate caffeine exposure improved reward-finding over successive visits. The improvement was associated with straighter foodward routes rather than a general increase in walking speed. The source recording follows an individual ant receiving 250 ppm caffeine. Its route preserves the turns and pauses that contribute to journey duration. Population-level comparisons across the experimental treatments established the relationship between concentration and foraging performance.

slides.title: Caffeine concentration changes foodward routes
body: The foodward route changed differently across caffeine concentrations. Ants receiving low or intermediate caffeine found the reward more efficiently with repeated visits. Ants given sucrose alone showed little comparable improvement. The highest tested concentration, 2000 ppm, also failed to retain the moderate-dose benefit. The response therefore followed a concentration-dependent pattern rather than a uniform stimulant effect.

Researchers tracked where an ant walked throughout the arena. A direct route required less travel than a route containing wide detours. Improved straightness shortened the journey even without a rise in walking speed. The source trajectories retained the spatial organization of the search. Repeated experience and pharmacological exposure acted together on the route used to obtain food.

The embedded recording follows a later visit by the same 250 ppm ant used in the earlier clip. Comparing visits preserves individual identity while displaying successive foraging attempts. A single trajectory remains one instance within the broader experiment. The primary analysis compared changes across many repeated journeys and treatment groups. Caffeine’s measured benefit concerned how the ants reached food, not an indiscriminate acceleration of movement.

slides.title: Repeated journeys change reward-finding time
body: The time needed to find a reward decreased across successive visits under moderate caffeine exposure. At low and intermediate concentrations, the reported improvement was approximately 38% per consecutive visit. Untreated ants did not exhibit the same consistent reduction. The very high concentration removed the improvement found at moderate doses. **Dose dependence** can therefore include a loss of benefit as exposure increases.

Foodward time includes departures, turns, pauses and detours before arrival. Walking speed describes movement during the path rather than the entire search outcome. Measuring both prevented a shorter journey from being attributed automatically to stronger motor activation. The trajectories linked reduced search time to more efficient travel. The reward’s fixed location supplied information that the ant could reuse on later visits.

The accompanying source recording follows an ant in the 2000 ppm condition. Its movement supplies a concrete example of foraging under the high-concentration treatment. The quantitative comparison concerns the distribution of repeated journeys across treatments. A compound that improves learning at moderate exposure need not improve performance at every exposure. The observed concentration range connects pharmacological action to the ecological task of locating food.

slides.title: Nestward and foodward journeys respond differently
body: Returning to the nest imposed a different navigational task from finding the food reward. After feeding, an ant traveled toward the nest entrance. Galante and colleagues analyzed these nestward trajectories separately from foodward journeys. Caffeine did not produce the same improvement in homing performance. Direction of travel therefore changed the behavioral expression of the treatment effect.

The outward and return journeys occurred in the same experimental setting. They differed in destination and in the information available after feeding. Separating them retained the functional distinction between obtaining food and carrying resources home. A general locomotor stimulant would be expected to affect movement more broadly. The measured improvement was concentrated in the foodward search instead.

The source recording follows another return visit by an ant receiving 2000 ppm caffeine. Its preserved sequence includes the movements that generated the recorded trajectory. Learning the route to a reward and navigating back to the nest responded differently to the same experimental exposure.

slides.title: Oriental hornets tolerate unusually strong ethanol
body: Oriental hornets, _Vespa orientalis_, tolerate ethanol concentrations that strongly affect many other animals. **Ethanol** is the alcohol produced when microorganisms ferment sugars. Bouchebti and colleagues supplied hornets with ethanol-containing solutions over repeated days. Their treatments extended to 80% ethanol. They assessed survival and behavior rather than assuming that consumption implied obvious intoxication.

Nest construction remained detectable across the tested concentration groups. Researchers measured the production of nest material during the experimental period. They also introduced an intruder and measured agonistic responses. **Agonistic behavior** includes actions associated with conflict, such as approaching and confronting another animal. Neither construction nor these confrontation measures declined systematically with increasing ethanol concentration in the tested conditions.

Survival comparisons also indicated an unusually high tolerance. The investigators tested workers and males and examined newly emerged workers over longer exposure. Hornets consumed substantial amounts rather than maintaining a fixed low ethanol intake through strict avoidance. Behavioral persistence was therefore accompanied by actual access and consumption. The physiological handling of ethanol supplies a complementary explanation for this extreme tolerance.

slides.title: Ethanol tolerance includes rapid metabolic handling
body: Ethanol metabolism converts the ingested compound into other molecules that can enter energy metabolism. The hornet study followed ethanol labeled with **carbon-13**, a stable carbon isotope. A stable isotope is a non-radioactive form of an element that can be distinguished by its mass. Researchers measured labeled carbon in exhaled carbon dioxide. This traced the processing of ethanol-derived carbon within the animal.

Hornets metabolized the labeled ethanol more rapidly than the compared honeybees. Measurements included several hornet life stages and worker bees. Label also appeared in hornet body tissues after ingestion. Ethanol therefore entered metabolic pathways rather than merely passing through the digestive system unchanged. The tracer measurements linked high behavioral tolerance to efficient chemical processing.

The investigators also compared genes encoding **alcohol dehydrogenase**, an enzyme involved in alcohol metabolism. Several _Vespa_ species carried multiple copies of the examined alcohol dehydrogenase gene. The authors propose that these copies may contribute to the hornets’ metabolic capacity. Gene copy number was a candidate mechanism rather than a direct experimental deletion of the copies. Behavioral tests, isotope tracing and genomic comparison addressed distinct components of the tolerance phenotype.

slides.title: Tree frogs learn associations with amphetamine
body: Male green tree frogs, _Hyla cinerea_, learned to prefer a context paired with amphetamine. **Amphetamine** increases monoamine signaling and acts as an indirect dopamine agonist. An **agonist** increases signaling through a receptor system, directly or through the available transmitter. Presley and colleagues paired the drug with a compartment that the frog initially avoided. The alternative compartment was paired with vehicle treatment.

The conditioning period lasted 14 d. Frogs in the drug group received 20 mg/kg amphetamine during the assigned pairings. Comparison frogs received vehicle in both contexts. After conditioning, drug-treated frogs shifted their preference toward the previously non-preferred context. Vehicle-treated animals did not display the same reversal of their initial preference.

The later test measured where the frog spent time when it could choose between contexts. The learned change persisted beyond the individual training episode. **Conditioned place preference** names this association between a context and the effects of a treatment. It differs from an animal performing an action to obtain the drug itself. In this amphibian, drug exposure altered the learned value of environmental cues.

slides.title: Place conditioning measures a learned context choice
body: The tree-frog place-conditioning experiment began with a strong baseline preference. Frogs could choose between compartments with different visual features. Researchers measured each animal’s allocation of time before drug pairing. The initially non-preferred compartment then became the amphetamine-associated context. This design tested whether experience could overcome an existing environmental preference.

A **context** is the combined set of environmental cues accompanying an experience. In this preparation, the compartments supplied distinct cues during drug and vehicle sessions. The comparison group experienced the apparatus and injections without amphetamine. Its stable preference separated ordinary repeated exposure from the drug-associated change. The critical outcome was a shift in where the animal subsequently chose to remain.

Preference was assessed with free access to both sides of the apparatus. The drug-associated context gained behavioral value despite starting as the less attractive option. Time allocation consequently reflected the history of the pairing. The study extended a reward-learning procedure to an amphibian species. Its experimental outcome concerned learned context selection rather than the frog’s momentary level of motor activation.

slides.title: Locomotor effects and conditioned preference differ
body: Amphetamine can change locomotion as well as the value of a learned context. The tree-frog study measured movement in a separate open-field assay. Frogs received vehicle, 10 mg/kg amphetamine or 20 mg/kg amphetamine. Researchers recorded their movement and other visible behaviors after treatment. The tested doses did not produce a clear increase in these motor measures.

The place-conditioning result therefore occurred without a parallel stimulant response in the open field. **Locomotor activation** means increased movement, whereas conditioned preference means changed allocation of time between learned contexts. These outcomes require different measurements. A drug can influence learning-related behavior without increasing every measured action. The frog results separated those two behavioral consequences under the tested conditions.

The movement assay used an arena rather than a choice between drug-paired compartments. It assessed immediate behavioral expression after the administered dose. The conditioning assay instead accumulated experience across repeated pairings. Different time scales and task demands exposed different effects of the same substance. In these frogs, the strongest measured consequence was altered context preference after training.

slides.title: Ethanol sensitivity depends on dopamine signaling
body: The nematode _Caenorhabditis elegans_ changes its movement under ethanol exposure. Pandey and colleagues examined animals lacking **DOP-2**, a D2-like dopamine receptor. Dopamine is a transmitter that modulates the activity of other neurons. A receptor converts the presence of a transmitter into a cellular response. The mutation altered the way an identified signaling system influenced intoxicated movement.

The researchers exposed worms to 400 mM ethanol in the external medium. This bath concentration is distinct from the concentration inside the animal. Wild-type worms continued to generate coordinated body movements under the assay conditions. Mutant worms increasingly dragged the posterior body while moving in circles. The study termed this pattern ethanol-induced sedative behavior.

The original wild-type recording preserves movement after prolonged ethanol exposure. It provides the behavioral comparison for the mutant and intervention recordings. Researchers quantified posture and movement rather than assigning a human psychological state to the worm. Genetic restoration of receptor function tested whether the altered behavior depended on DOP-2. A compact nervous system allowed the pathway from transmitter regulation to motor output to be examined cell by cell.

slides.title: DOP-2 loss changes the movement response to ethanol
body: DOP-2 acts as a dopamine **autoreceptor**, a receptor through which a dopamine neuron regulates its own signaling. Such feedback can limit transmitter output. Removing the receptor can therefore increase downstream dopamine signaling rather than simply remove all dopamine effects. The worm experiment tested this relationship during ethanol exposure. The mutant’s circular movement combined abnormal posture with reduced effective forward travel.

Restoring DOP-2 in dopaminergic neurons improved the movement phenotype. The investigators also examined other dopamine-pathway mutants. Reducing dopamine production suppressed the abnormal response associated with DOP-2 loss. These interventions placed dopamine availability upstream of the observed motor pattern. The phenotype depended on both the receptor genotype and the ethanol condition.

The mutant recording contains the dragging and turning described in the assay. Its posterior body fails to contribute the coordinated movement seen in wild type. The difference concerns the organization of a motor sequence, not merely total displacement. Ethanol exposed a regulatory function of dopamine feedback within the locomotor circuit. Receptor loss changed the amount of signaling reaching the rest of that circuit.

slides.title: PDE neurons contribute to ethanol-dependent sedation
body: The worm’s posterior dopamine neurons, named **PDE**, contributed strongly to the ethanol-induced movement defect. These sensory neurons are positioned in the posterior part of the animal. Pandey and colleagues manipulated the cells within the identified dopamine system. Restoring DOP-2 function in the relevant neurons reduced the abnormal behavior. The experiment localized a functional contribution within the small nervous system.

Ablating PDE neurons also suppressed the mutant phenotype. **Ablation** removes or destroys a selected cell so that its contribution can be tested. The intervention reduced the dopamine source implicated in excessive signaling. The accompanying recording contains a mutant animal after this cell-specific manipulation. More coordinated movement followed removal of the relevant neurons despite the continued ethanol condition.

The result places the posterior dopamine cells upstream of the altered motor output. Their effect was not inferred only from where a fluorescent label appeared. Cell-specific restoration and cell removal supplied complementary interventions. Increased dopamine release during ethanol exposure provided a chemical link to the behavior. The pathway converted the state of a small sensory-neuron population into a whole-body movement pattern.

slides.title: Dopamine and ethanol interact within a motor circuit
body: Adding dopamine to wild-type worms tested whether increased transmitter could reproduce the mutant response. The animals were examined with and without ethanol. Dopamine alone did not produce the same sedative movement pattern. Dopamine combined with ethanol generated abnormal locomotion resembling the DOP-2 mutant phenotype. The outcome depended on an interaction between the transmitter condition and the drug exposure.

The study measured dopamine release using a fluorescent secretion reporter in PDE neurons. A **reporter** produces a detectable signal linked to the process being measured. In this preparation, changes in the reporter reflected vesicle release from the dopamine cells. Ethanol exposure increased the measured release in the receptor mutant. The chemical measurement supported the pathway inferred from genetic and behavioral interventions.

The paired recordings preserve the dopamine-only and dopamine-plus-ethanol conditions. Coordinated movement in the first condition contrasts with abnormal movement in the second. DOP-2 feedback normally regulates the signal available to downstream cells. Removing that restraint changes the circuit’s response during ethanol exposure. The behavioral state consequently arises from the combination of pharmacological exposure and transmitter regulation.

slides.title: Neuropeptide signaling changes motor output
body: The worm pathway continued through **DVA**, an interneuron that links sensory information to motor regulation. An interneuron relays and transforms signals within a neural circuit. DVA releases **NLP-12**, a neuropeptide that modulates locomotion. A neuropeptide is a small protein signal released by neurons. Pandey and colleagues tested whether this cell and peptide carried the consequences of excess dopamine.

Removing DVA function or reducing NLP-12 suppressed the abnormal ethanol response. Conversely, increased NLP-12 expression promoted the sedative movement phenotype. D1-like dopamine signaling contributed to the downstream effect. The pathway therefore included dopamine reception by a different cell from the one releasing dopamine. Transmitter feedback in PDE and downstream excitation were distinct steps in the circuit.

NLP-12 acted through signaling that altered cholinergic motor output. **Cholinergic** neurons release acetylcholine, the transmitter used to activate worm body-wall muscle. Excess modulation disrupted the coordinated bending that normally advances the animal. The source recording contains an NLP-12-overexpressing worm under ethanol exposure. Its motor pattern connects peptide signaling to the movement outcome measured across the genetic interventions.

body: Fruit flies respond to ethanol vapor with a sequence of different motor states. Kong and colleagues first observed a brief odor-triggered startle response. A quieter interval preceded a more sustained period of increased walking. Peak hyperactivity occurred approximately 10–12 min after exposure began. Continued ethanol accumulation eventually produced incoordination and sedation.

The investigators blocked transmitter release from dopamine neurons using a genetically targeted toxin. The sustained hyperactive phase was reduced. The initial odor-startle response remained comparatively intact. These outcomes separated the sensory detection of ethanol vapor from its later locomotor effect. **Hyperactivity** here denotes elevated walking speed during the defined intoxication phase.

A small group of dopamine neurons in the **PPM3** cluster projected toward the central complex. The central complex is a set of insect brain structures involved in organizing movement. Genetic activation and inactivation implicated this restricted pathway in ethanol-stimulated walking. The source confocal recording preserves the labeled neuronal projections in three dimensions. Anatomical targeting and behavioral intervention connected dopamine release to a specific motor-control pathway.

slides.title: DopR function links a brain target to intoxication
body: The **ellipsoid body** is a ring-shaped component of the fly central complex. It receives projections from the dopamine neurons implicated in ethanol hyperactivity. Kong and colleagues examined **DopR**, a D1-like dopamine receptor, in this target region. A D1-like receptor activates intracellular signaling after dopamine binds. Receptor location consequently determines which target cells respond to the released transmitter.

DopR mutant flies exhibited reduced ethanol-stimulated hyperactivity. Reintroducing receptor function in the appropriate ellipsoid-body neurons improved the response. Rescue in selected cells tested where receptor activity could restore the behavior. The investigators distinguished these effects from baseline movement and the initial odor startle. The receptor contribution concerned a specific component of the intoxication sequence.

The study’s labeled brain preparations identified receptor expression and the associated neuronal populations. Dopamine release and DopR reception occupied successive positions in the proposed functional pathway. Manipulating either position altered the walking response. The experiment connected a molecular receptor with anatomically restricted target cells. Ethanol-dependent behavior therefore depended on which cells received dopamine, as well as on the presence of the transmitter.

slides.title: Repeated ethanol exposure changes fly courtship
body: Repeated ethanol exposure changed male fruit-fly courtship in Lee and colleagues’ experiments. Untreated males ordinarily direct most courtship toward females. Following repeated daily exposure, males increasingly courted other males during intoxication. The researchers recorded orientation, following and other components of the courtship sequence. These actions supplied a defined behavioral measure of disinhibition.

The response strengthened across repeated exposures, a pattern called **behavioral sensitization**. Sensitization is an increased response after earlier experience with a substance. The same flies also developed tolerance to ethanol’s sedating effects. Stronger courtship and reduced sedation therefore emerged together under recurring exposure. Different components of intoxication changed in different directions.

The original recording compares behavior before exposure and during early and later ethanol sessions. Courtship after repeated treatment differed from the initial drug response. Manipulations of dopamine signaling reduced the ethanol-induced intermale courtship. The circuit controlling courtship remained necessary for the disinhibited action sequence. Repeated drug experience recruited an existing social behavior under conditions that ordinarily elicited little of it.

slides.title: Genetic background modifies ethanol disinhibition
body: The fly courtship response depended on genetic background as well as ethanol history. Lee and colleagues examined the **white** gene, which encodes a transporter-associated protein best known for its role in eye pigmentation. Its effects extend beyond the visible eye phenotype. Males lacking normal white function exhibited a reduced disinhibited courtship response. The researchers compared mutant and genetically restored animals under repeated ethanol exposure.

Restoring white expression increased the intermale courtship response under the tested conditions. The recording preserves the behavioral contrast between the compared genotypes. Genetic rescue links the phenotype to the manipulated gene more directly than a comparison of unrelated fly strains. The measured actions were components of courtship rather than an undifferentiated increase in movement. Genotype changed which behavior emerged during intoxication.

The study also tested genes and signaling pathways involved in ordinary courtship control. **Fruitless** is a gene involved in organizing male courtship circuitry. Disrupting this pathway reduced the drug-associated courtship response. Ethanol therefore acted through an existing behavioral organization rather than creating an entirely new action sequence. Repeated exposure, transmitter signaling and genetic background jointly determined the social outcome.

slides.title: A first ethanol experience leaves a neural memory
body: A first sedating ethanol exposure can change the response to a later exposure in fruit flies. Larnerd and colleagues separated several forms of this tolerance. **Rapid tolerance** develops after an earlier drug episode and is measured during a subsequent challenge. A cold-shock intervention removed part of the early tolerance response. The remaining component persisted despite that intervention.

The researchers named these components **anesthesia-sensitive tolerance** and **anesthesia-resistant tolerance**. Their contributions differed between tests at 4 h and 24 h. The gene **amnesiac**, associated with memory processes, contributed to the sensitive component. The gene **radish** contributed to the resistant component. Distinct genetic requirements separated adaptations that would otherwise be combined in one behavioral score.

The **mushroom bodies** contain Kenyon cells that participate in fly learning. Manipulations of these cells affected particular tolerance components. Other required encoding steps were located outside the mushroom bodies. Tolerance was therefore distributed across more than one cell population and signaling process. An earlier ethanol episode left several experimentally separable effects on later drug responsiveness.

slides.title: GABA circuits distinguish forms of ethanol tolerance
body: **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an inhibitory transmitter in the fly brain. The anterior paired lateral neurons, abbreviated **APL**, provide GABAergic regulation within the mushroom-body system. Larnerd and colleagues manipulated their activity during different phases of ethanol exposure. The timing of the manipulation separated acquisition of tolerance from later expression. A neuron could contribute while the adaptation formed without serving the same role during its measurement.

Reducing APL activity during acquisition decreased rapid tolerance. The investigators also altered GABA-related signaling in Kenyon cells. These interventions distinguished the early tolerance components from adaptations produced by a longer low-concentration exposure. **Chronic tolerance** here refers to that prolonged-exposure condition. Its dependence on protein synthesis and circuit activity differed from the short-exposure forms.

Inhibitory signaling can regulate whether experience produces a lasting change in responsiveness. The relevant cells were components of the same broad learning system but participated differently across conditions. Exposure duration and the time of intervention consequently mattered alongside cell identity. The original anatomical labels locate the manipulated neurons relative to the mushroom bodies. Separate cellular requirements explain why a single total-tolerance score can conceal multiple adaptations.

slides.title: Zebrafish can obtain an opioid through their actions
body: Adult zebrafish learned to obtain hydrocodone by swimming across an active platform. **Hydrocodone** is an opioid, a substance acting at opioid receptors. Bosse and colleagues used a group self-administration assay in which crossing the platform delivered drug locally. An inactive platform provided a comparison without the same delivery consequence. The animal’s action therefore controlled exposure through a defined contingency.

**Self-administration** means that the subject performs an action that produces delivery of the substance. This differs from an injection scheduled by the experimenter. Fish were conditioned over 4 d before candidate treatments were tested. The later session measured platform activations over 30 min. Comparing active and inactive responses retained information about the learned drug-associated action.

The researchers screened compounds for their ability to reduce the active-platform response. Methadone, a clinically used opioid treatment, reduced hydrocodone self-administration in this assay. Finasteride also reduced responding after pretreatment. **Finasteride** inhibits an enzyme involved in steroid metabolism. The screen connected an action-based drug-taking measure with a molecular pathway outside the opioid receptor itself.

slides.title: Drug seeking can change without suppressing all behavior
body: Finasteride reduced zebrafish self-administration of several opioids. The researchers tested hydrocodone, morphine and fentanyl after conditioning. The reduction was concentrated in responses at the active platform. Responses at the inactive platform supplied a separate movement-related comparison. A lower drug-associated response was therefore examined alongside behavior that did not deliver opioid.

Researchers also measured general locomotion and feeding after finasteride treatment. Those behaviors remained available under conditions that reduced opioid self-administration. This control changes the interpretation of the reduced active-platform response. A treatment that simply immobilized the fish would suppress several behaviors at once. Finasteride’s profile instead separated the drug-related response from broad motor or feeding suppression.

The targeted enzyme, **5α-reductase**, participates in producing neuroactive steroids. **Neuroactive steroids** are steroid molecules that influence nervous-system signaling. Fish brain measurements detected increased dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate after finasteride treatment. Related precursor treatments also reduced opioid self-administration. The authors propose that altered steroid metabolism contributes to the behavioral effect, and tested corresponding drug-taking outcomes in rats.

slides.title: Nicotine produces a concentration-dependent response
body: Larval zebrafish respond to nicotine with concentration-dependent changes in swimming. Petzold and colleagues measured movement using digital imaging. A water stimulus supplied the baseline comparison. Low and intermediate nicotine concentrations increased the locomotor response. Higher concentrations reduced activity relative to the peak response, producing an inverted-U concentration profile.

The researchers selected 10 μM nicotine for much of the subsequent assay. A functional acute response was present at 4 d after fertilization but not at 3 d. **Developmental competence** means that the relevant behavioral response has become available at that age. The emergence of nicotine responsiveness therefore depended on maturation. Concentration alone did not predict the outcome without information about developmental stage.

Nicotine activates **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors**, ion channels opened by binding of an appropriate chemical signal. Opening these channels changes the electrical activity of responsive cells. The antagonist mecamylamine blocked nicotine-induced locomotor activation. It did not produce the same reduction in baseline movement. The pharmacological comparison linked the measured swimming response to nicotinic receptor signaling.

slides.title: Repeated nicotine exposure changes later responsiveness
body: Prior nicotine exposure increased the response to a later nicotine challenge in zebrafish larvae. The investigators called this effect **sensitization**, an enhanced response following earlier treatment. Acute responsiveness and sensitization appeared at different developmental stages. Five- and six-day-old larvae could express the sensitized response. Four-day-old larvae responded acutely but did not yet exhibit the same sensitization.

The study tested whether glutamate receptor signaling contributed to this adaptation. **Glutamate** is an excitatory transmitter, and NMDA receptors are one class of its receptors. The antagonist APV interferes with NMDA-receptor activation. Coadministration during nicotine exposure prevented the development of sensitization. The intervention separated the response to nicotine from the processes that changed later responsiveness.

Repeated exposure consequently recruited more than the receptor directly activated by nicotine. Cholinergic signaling supplied the initial drug-sensitive pathway. NMDA-receptor involvement connected prior exposure with a later behavioral change. The locomotor recordings retain the assay’s swimming movements and temporal pattern. Behavioral history and developmental stage determined how strongly the same nicotine concentration altered movement.

slides.title: A genetic screen separates nicotine-response pathways
body: Petzold and colleagues used the nicotine assay to identify genes affecting drug responsiveness. A **forward genetic screen** begins with altered behavior and then identifies the associated genetic change. Gene-breaking transposons disrupted selected genes while supplying fluorescent tags. A **transposon** is a DNA element that can insert into another genomic location. The tag allowed researchers to track inherited insertions through families.

The screen excluded lines with obvious baseline swimming defects. Remaining candidates were tested for altered acute and sensitized nicotine responses. One affected gene was **cct8**, which encodes a component of a protein-folding complex. Its mutant line was named bette davis. These fish had reduced nicotine responses while retaining responses to several other tested stimuli.

The investigators followed the insertion through breeding and molecular analysis. They measured the reduction in intact gene transcript and examined its expression in neural tissue. These steps connected the behavioral phenotype to a defined genomic location. The source figures preserve neural expression and the resulting movement-response comparisons. A drug-responsive behavior can identify cellular machinery beyond the receptor to which the drug initially binds.

slides.title: GABA-B signaling contributes to nicotine responses
body: A second zebrafish nicotine-response mutation affected **gabbr1.2**, a gene encoding a GABA-B receptor subunit. GABA-B receptors signal through G proteins rather than forming the rapidly opening channel characteristic of GABA-A receptors. A **G protein** relays receptor activation to intracellular signaling pathways. The mutant line was named humphrey bogart. Its nicotine response was strongly reduced despite relatively preserved baseline movement.

The gene-breaking insertion also supplied a red fluorescent reporter. Neural labeling located expression associated with the disrupted locus. Researchers then used **Cre recombinase**, an enzyme that cuts DNA at specified recognition sites, to remove the disruptive cassette. Reversing the insertion restored the nicotine-response phenotype toward normal. This reversal supplied a direct test linking the genomic intervention with behavior.

The original three-dimensional recording contains the red reporter-labeled neural preparation. Its fluorescence identifies the cells carrying the tagged expression pattern. The behavioral rescue and anatomical expression address complementary questions about the affected pathway. GABA-B signaling contributed to how the larva responded to a cholinergic drug. Nicotine responsiveness therefore depended on interactions among transmitter systems rather than on nicotinic receptors alone.

slides.title: A partner’s drinking changes the vole social context
body: Prairie voles, _Microtus ochrogaster_, can maintain a preference for a familiar mating partner. Walcott and Ryabinin allowed pairs to cohabit for 1 week before manipulating alcohol access. Males then received access to water and 10% ethanol. Their partners either received the same choice or water alone. A control condition supplied water to both members of the pair.

**Concordant drinking** means that both partners have access to alcohol in this design. **Discordant drinking** means that alcohol access differs between partners. The comparison changed the social context of the male’s drinking. Males whose partners also received alcohol consumed more than males whose partners received only water. Amount consumed and the later social preference were measured separately.

The partner-preference test offered a familiar partner and an unfamiliar female. Investigators measured time spent huddling with each animal. Huddling is sustained close bodily contact rather than simple occupancy of the same chamber. All treatment groups retained a measurable partner preference. The strength of that preference was lower when only the male had alcohol access.

slides.title: Discordant alcohol intake alters partner preference
body: Discordant drinking reduced male prairie voles’ partner preference relative to the comparison conditions. The effect occurred after the relationship had already formed. The experiment therefore examined **pair-bond maintenance**, the persistence of an established selective attachment. It differed from testing whether a new pair bond could form during intoxication. The partner’s drinking condition altered the outcome of the male’s alcohol exposure.

Both-drinking pairs retained a stronger partner preference than pairs in which only the male drank. Alcohol consumption alone consequently did not predict the social outcome. Researchers also measured drinking outside the immediate presence of the partner. The preference difference remained associated with the treatment history. The social effect reflected more than the male merely approaching another animal during simultaneous drinking.

The study examined **oxytocin**, a neuropeptide involved in social regulation, in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus. Alcohol-exposed males had reduced oxytocin immunoreactivity in this region. This reduction occurred regardless of the female partner’s drinking status. **Immunoreactivity** measures the signal detected by an antibody directed at the target molecule. The shared oxytocin change therefore differed from the partner-dependent behavioral pattern.

slides.title: Alcohol affects different social behaviors differently
body: Aggression and partner preference were assessed with different social tests in the prairie vole study. A **resident–intruder test** places an unfamiliar animal into the subject’s environment. Researchers counted aggressive responses toward a stranger male. Aggression frequency did not differ clearly across the drinking conditions. The partner-preference difference therefore did not generalize to every measured social behavior.

The researchers also examined FosB-family protein signals in the **periaqueductal gray**, a midbrain region surrounding the cerebral aqueduct. Males in the discordant-drinking condition had increased FosB immunoreactivity there. Both-drinking males did not display the same regional increase. This molecular pattern corresponded more closely to the partner-dependent preference effect than did the shared oxytocin reduction. The measurement supplied a candidate neural association for the social difference.

An antibody signal identifies a protein-related response within sampled cells. It does not by itself establish that the region caused the change in attachment. The behavioral comparisons nevertheless separated selective contact with a partner from aggression toward a stranger. Region-specific measurements further separated common alcohol effects from partner-dependent ones. The animal’s social environment altered which behavioral and neural outcomes accompanied its drinking history.

slides.title: Social rank influences reinstatement in macaques
body: Socially housed cynomolgus macaques, _Macaca fascicularis_, learned to choose between drug-associated and food-associated options. Roberts and colleagues examined **reinstatement**, the return of a previously reduced drug-associated response. Saline replaced drug during extinction sessions. **Extinction** is the decline in responding when its previous consequence is removed. Later drug pretreatment tested whether the response returned.

Cocaine and **cocaethylene** both increased choice of the previously drug-associated option. Cocaethylene is an active metabolite formed when cocaine and ethanol are used together. Cocaine produced reinstatement at lower doses than cocaethylene in the comparison. The study examined socially dominant and subordinate animals of both sexes. Dominant animals generally displayed greater reinstatement than subordinates under these conditions.

Social rank was therefore relevant to a specific stage of drug-related behavior. The measured outcome was renewed drug-associated choice after extinction. It was not a general ranking of which social group was always most vulnerable to every drug effect. Food remained an available alternative during the choice procedure. The assay connected social position with competition between a drug-associated action and another reinforced action.

slides.title: Nicotine changes cocaine-related responding by sex
body: Nicotine altered cocaine-related reinstatement differently in male and female macaques. Roberts and colleagues tested nicotine alone and together with cocaine or cocaethylene. The drug-associated choice measure was the same response used during extinction and reinstatement. Nicotine alone increased that choice primarily in females. Its effect consequently depended on the subject’s sex and the existing history of the drug-associated option.

Adding nicotine increased cocaine-induced drug-associated choice in females more consistently than in males. The tested nicotine range was 0.01–0.056 mg/kg. The corresponding interaction with cocaethylene did not produce the same clear group effect. **Polysubstance exposure** means exposure to more than one psychoactive substance. Interactions between substances were specific rather than interchangeable across the tested combinations.

Social rank did not account for the female-selective nicotine effect. Both dominant and subordinate females could display enhanced cocaine-related responding. Sex and rank therefore contributed differently to the experimental outcomes. The task retained food as the competing alternative rather than measuring movement alone. A social and biological context can alter which action is selected after renewed exposure to a drug combination.

slides.title: A single intoxication changes neuronal organization
body: A single ethanol intoxication altered neuronal proteins and organization in mice. Knabbe and colleagues first measured proteins associated with hippocampal synapses. A **synapse** is a specialized contact through which a neuron communicates with another cell. Several proteins changed their abundance in the synaptic preparation after ethanol exposure. The affected proteins included molecules involved in neuronal structure and mitochondrial function.

The investigators then examined selected changes in living-animal preparations and stained tissue. **Ankyrin-G** helps organize the axon initial segment, the specialized region near the start of the axon. The axon carries signals away from the neuronal cell body. Ethanol changed synaptic ankyrin-G abundance and altered the length of the initial segment in the tested preparation. The molecular screen therefore led to measurements of a defined neuronal structure.

The study also followed organelles within cortical axons using repeated microscopy. **Mitochondria** support cellular energy metabolism and can move along axons. Baseline imaging established which organelles were stationary or mobile before treatment. The source recording preserves this transport before the ethanol-associated change. Measurements within the same neuronal stretches connected the acute exposure with subsequent cellular dynamics.

slides.title: Ethanol increases mitochondrial mobility in axons
body: Ethanol increased the fraction of axonal mitochondria that moved in the mouse imaging experiment. Investigators repeatedly imaged labeled axons in the motor cortex. The **motor cortex** is a cerebral cortical region involved in movement control. Saline and ethanol sessions provided within-animal comparisons. Images were collected repeatedly over the hours following treatment.

The increase in mitochondrial mobility became apparent after approximately 60 min. It reached roughly twice the baseline level around 180 min. The effect persisted for at least 4 h but was absent at the 24 h measurement. **Mobility** here refers to the proportion of mitochondria moving during observation. The velocity of moving mitochondria did not increase in parallel.

The distinction separates recruitment into movement from faster transport once movement begins. A stationary mitochondrion can become mobile without changing the speed of the moving population. The ethanol-condition recording preserves the individual transport events used to assess this process. Repeated imaging retained the location and direction of movement within the same axons. Acute intoxication consequently changed organelle dynamics on a time scale extending beyond the immediate drug administration.

slides.title: Vesicle transport provides a distinct cellular comparison
body: The mouse study compared mitochondrial transport with transport of **dense-core vesicles**. These vesicles carry secreted neuronal materials in membrane-bound packages. Both vesicles and mitochondria can travel along **microtubules**, structural tracks within the axon. Measuring another cargo tested whether ethanol caused a general acceleration of axonal transport. The comparison used labeled vesicles in the same broad imaging approach.

Dense-core-vesicle mobility did not increase under the ethanol condition. Their transport velocity also remained similar across the compared conditions. Mitochondrial mobility therefore changed selectively relative to this cargo. The source recording preserves the vesicle movements used for that comparison. The result narrows the cellular effect from all axonal transport to a particular organelle process.

The investigators also examined mitochondrial trafficking in a separate fruit-fly reward-learning experiment. Reducing the transport-associated proteins Miro or Milton in dopamine neurons disrupted conditioned ethanol preference. Responses to a sucrose-associated reward supplied a separate learning comparison. Mouse organelle imaging and fly genetic intervention addressed related processes in different preparations. Together they connected ethanol exposure, neuronal cargo regulation and a measured drug-associated learned behavior.

slides.title: Repeated drug exposure recruits ΔFosB in defined neurons
body: **ΔFosB** is a shortened protein produced from an alternatively spliced transcript of the FosB gene. It acts as a **transcription factor**, a protein that regulates the expression of other genes. Repeated stimulation can change neuronal responses beyond an individual exposure. Lobo and colleagues measured ΔFosB in identified mouse striatal neurons after repeated drug treatment. Cell labeling distinguished populations mixed together in whole-tissue measurements.

**Medium spiny neurons** are inhibitory projection neurons named for the small protrusions on their dendrites. The **nucleus accumbens**, a ventral part of the striatum, contains core and shell subdivisions. The investigators distinguished neurons expressing D1-type dopamine receptors from those expressing D2-type receptors. Seven daily cocaine treatments increased ΔFosB predominantly in D1-type neurons in the examined striatal regions. Measurement 24 h after treatment separated persistent induction from immediate exposure.

Different substances recruited different cell populations in the same study. Voluntary cocaine self-administration also favored ΔFosB induction in D1-type neurons. Morphine treatment and heroin self-administration recruited both D1-type and D2-type populations. Sucrose exposure and environmental enrichment could also increase ΔFosB in both populations. Gene regulation depended on substance, cell population and exposure conditions.

slides.title: Phosphorylation helps ΔFosB resist degradation
body: **Protein half-life** is the time over which half of a labeled protein population disappears. Ulery and colleagues measured ΔFosB turnover using a pulse of labeled amino acids followed by an unlabeled chase. In PC12 cells, a rat-derived neuron-like preparation, ΔFosB had a half-life of approximately 10 h. Full-length FosB was already known to turn over much faster in cell culture. These measurements concern cellular protein persistence rather than behavioral duration.

**Phosphorylation** adds a phosphate group to a protein and can change its interactions or stability. The investigators identified serine at position 27, termed **Ser27**, as a stabilizing phosphorylation site. Replacing serine with alanine prevented phosphorylation there. In PC12 cells, this substitution shortened the measured half-life from approximately 11 h to approximately 4 h. Mimicking the phosphate’s negative charge instead increased stability.

A **proteasome** is a cellular complex that breaks down selected proteins. Two different proteasome inhibitors reversed the accelerated loss of the alanine-substituted ΔFosB protein. The altered amino acid affected this degradation pathway. The study also identified **casein kinase 2**, an enzyme that transfers phosphate groups, as a regulator of Ser27 phosphorylation. Protein stabilization supplies a molecular mechanism through which repeated activation can sustain a transcriptional response after the initiating stimulus has ended.

slides.title: ΔFosB and CaMKII couple gene regulation to plasticity
body: **CaMKII** is calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, an enzyme whose activation links calcium signals to protein phosphorylation. Robison and colleagues examined its relationship with ΔFosB in the nucleus accumbens. Repeated cocaine exposure in rats increased CaMKII particularly in the accumbens shell under the tested conditions. ΔFosB promoted expression of the gene encoding the alpha form of CaMKII in D1-type neurons. This transcriptional relationship connects a persistent nuclear protein with a signaling enzyme that acts within neurons.

The investigators manipulated ΔFosB using viral expression in mouse accumbens neurons. Increasing ΔFosB increased the density of **dendritic spines**, small neuronal protrusions that receive many excitatory synaptic contacts. Coexpressing a peptide inhibitor of CaMKII prevented this structural effect. The manipulation also prevented the ΔFosB-associated enhancement of cocaine locomotion. The interventions connected this pathway to neuronal structure and drug-related behavior.

CaMKII also phosphorylated ΔFosB at Ser27, linking the kinase back to the transcription factor’s stability. The proteins formed a positive regulatory loop in this preparation. **Sensitization** refers here to an increased behavioral response following repeated drug exposure. Cocaine-induced locomotion supplied the behavioral measurement alongside molecular and structural changes. Cell identity and accumbens subregion determine where this particular loop is engaged.

slides.title: Social stress recruits different ΔFosB cell populations
body: Lobo and colleagues exposed mice to 10 d of repeated social defeat and then measured their social interaction. **Susceptible** animals displayed reduced interaction under the study’s behavioral classification. **Resilient** animals maintained social interaction despite exposure to the same defeat procedure. Researchers measured ΔFosB in D1-type and D2-type medium spiny neurons separately. Separate measurements identified which population responded.

Susceptible mice had increased ΔFosB in D2-type neurons in accumbens core, accumbens shell and dorsal striatum. Resilient mice instead had increased ΔFosB in D1-type neurons in those regions. Measurement followed defeat and social-interaction assessment. Opposite behavioral outcomes accompanied induction in different populations. Total ΔFosB alone would omit this cell-type distinction.

The study also examined repeated treatment with **fluoxetine**, an antidepressant that inhibits serotonin reuptake. Fourteen days of treatment increased ΔFosB predominantly in D1-type neurons in the examined striatal regions. Cocaine, resilience and antidepressant treatment shared a cell-type pattern under different conditions. ΔFosB is part of experience-dependent gene regulation across rewarding, stressful and pharmacological contexts. The behavioral meaning of its induction depends on the cells and the experience that recruited it.

slides.title: Human ΔFosB findings depend on the sampled brain region
body: Human research compared postmortem tissue from cocaine-dependent and comparison subjects. Robison and colleagues found increased ΔFosB and CaMKII in the sampled human nucleus accumbens. Rodent interventions linked these proteins to cocaine-responsive cellular and behavioral changes. Human measurements identified a corresponding regional molecular association. Postmortem comparisons leave its timing relative to drug use unresolved.

Gajewski and colleagues examined two additional regions: the **hippocampus**, involved in memory processing, and the **prefrontal cortex**, involved in the regulation of behavior. A **Western blot**, an antibody-based assay, separated FosB-family proteins by molecular mass. Cocaine-dependent subjects had lower hippocampal ΔFosB and other FosB-family signals. The sampled prefrontal cortex did not exhibit the same group differences. The direction of the finding depended on the sampled region.

The hippocampal samples also had reduced **GluA2**, a subunit of AMPA-type receptors that carry excitatory glutamate signals. Reduced GluA2 accompanied the altered FosB-family pattern. Human and mouse samples shared major FosB-family protein bands, while human tissue contained additional detected bands. Mouse controls tested whether delayed collection explained those additional signals. Regional sampling and protein identification shape comparisons between animal mechanisms and human observations.

items.text: Drug administration, conditioned preference and self-administration measure different behavioral processes.
Caffeine, nicotine and ethanol can improve one response while impairing another; dose and task determine the effect.
Dopamine feedback, target receptors and neuropeptide signaling link molecular interventions to organized animal behavior.
Tolerance and sensitization can coexist and depend on different genes, circuits and time scales.
Partner drinking, social rank and sex change selective social responses or renewed drug-associated choice.

items.lead: ΔFosB links experience to gene regulation.
items.text: Its stability and cell-specific induction connect repeated exposure with plasticity; human findings depend on the sampled brain region.
